name: Bianca Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and lead a small tax and accounts review team. I like finding the one missing receipt that changes a shop owner’s return; I do not like telling juniors to rush the checks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is on your mind when you leave the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, and my pay is low for a senior accountant. We have no children, but my savings cover less than a month and few similar jobs are close by. I use AI tools now and then after colleagues test them, though I still check every figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster software is useful if someone still checks the return before filing. My clients bring in crumpled receipts, so the last mile is rarely tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like trying a tool after somebody else has tested it, but this small change will not rescue my budget. I have less than one month saved and my pay is low for a senior accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would run one approved AI draft against my own tax checklist on a low-risk file and show the differences to my manager. I would keep my current client portfolio in the first year and set a standing transfer of 25 a week to savings if my hours stay full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a bit stretched already, even though this picture barely moves the job. If rent rises again, the clever software will not pay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would make you stop using the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed tax relief for a small shop would be enough to pause it. I would put the receipt next to the draft and ask a colleague to check my finding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much room is there in your weekly pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 25 a week when I pack lunch, and nothing if an unexpected bill comes in. Few nearby firms are hiring for the same kind of work.

say: I would say **faster drafts** help only if somebody checks returns before filing.
I would tell clients their **messy receipts** still need careful human review.
think: I am open to a **tested tool**, but small efficiencies will not fix my tight budget.
I have **less than a month** saved and few nearby firms to move to.
do: Compare one **approved AI draft** with my tax checklist on a low-risk file.
Keep my **client portfolio** and transfer 25 weekly to savings if hours hold.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent and my thin cushion despite stable work.
S0.quote: If rent rises again, the clever software will not pay it.
fieldNote: She is **curious but cautious**: she would test one approved draft against a checklist and another person’s review.
Her **weekly savings goal** depends on full hours, and ordinary rent pressure already makes her budget fragile.

steps.text: Compare one approved AI tax draft with personal checklist
Keep serving current client portfolio through first year
Transfer 25 weekly to savings if hours stay full

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm we should show clients where software made the first pass and where we checked it. Hiding that would only make a wrong tax figure worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tax notes and checking accounts fill most of my day, so fewer juniors could soon mean fewer senior hours too. I can learn a tool, but I cannot absorb a pay cut right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my manager to let me test the approved drafting tool on three returns, with another accountant checking the result. I would pack lunch four days a week and save 40 a week; in the first year I would ask to take on client calls about errors if that work opens up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but not frozen. A test gives me evidence, though it does not guarantee the payroll stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record from those three returns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log the time saved and each mistake, especially wrong tax codes or missing expenses. If the tool makes hidden errors, I want them on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about client calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask if those calls carry paid hours rather than extra work squeezed into the same week. My salary is already low for the qualification I hold.

say: I would ask our firm to **show clients** where software drafts and accountants check.
I would warn that hiding a **wrong tax figure** damages trust.
think: My **writing and checking** hours may shrink as the firm leaves vacancies unfilled.
I could learn the tool, but I cannot manage a **pay cut**.
do: Test approved drafting software on **three returns** with another accountant checking.
Pack lunch and save **40 weekly** while hours hold.
Ask for **paid client calls** about errors if the work opens.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though testing gives me something useful to do.
S1.quote: A test gives me evidence, though it does not guarantee the payroll stays the same.
fieldNote: She measures the tool by **logged errors** and time saved, a practical way to learn without assuming it is reliable.
Her interest in **client calls** is conditional on paid hours, because her senior title has not brought senior pay.

steps.text: Test approved drafting tool on three checked tax returns
Pack lunch and save 40 weekly while hours hold
Ask for paid client-call work if openings arise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches accounts and tax returns the moment it arrives. Waiting for capable robots around 2031 would be missing the date that matters to our office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a master’s degree and a chartered qualification, and I am good at this work, but the screen work could be done cheaper. With less than a month saved, losing hours would hit rent before I found another job nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners for a written schedule of expected staffing and paid training for tax hearings, where clients may still want a representative. I would enroll before 2028 if they approve the fees and paid hours in writing. I would stop weekend trips and save the fare; if my hours are cut in the first year after 2028, I would apply for the firm’s client liaison vacancy if it exists and ask my partner to cover more rent only for a month while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, because I can count the bills faster than I can count possible jobs. I am willing to learn, but two years is not much runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the partners first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for dates and numbers, not a promise that everyone is valued. A written hours forecast would tell me whether to plan for half a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you discuss rent with your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my partner the actual cut in hours and our rent bill, then agree on one month of help. I would not make an open-ended request when their pay also has limits.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax and accounts desks immediately.
I would tell colleagues that **2031 robots** do not delay our office risk.
think: My qualifications may not protect **screen work** when cheaper AGI arrives.
With **less than a month** saved, reduced hours would hit rent quickly.
do: Request a **written staffing forecast** and enroll in tax hearing training if partners approve fees and paid hours.
Cut **weekend trips** and save the fare before 2028.
Apply for a vacant **client liaison** post and seek one month of rent help after hours fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely income loss and few local accounting jobs.
S2.quote: I can count the bills faster than I can count possible jobs.
fieldNote: Her **willingness to learn** does not erase the 2028 cash gap; she asks for staffing numbers before making commitments.
The **partner rent request** is tightly limited to one month and depends on an actual hours cut, not a rumour.

steps.text: Enroll in tax hearing training if partners approve fees and paid hours in writing
Stop weekend trips and save fares before 2028
Apply for vacant firm client liaison post after hours fall
Ask partner for one month rent help after hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us time to test software properly and explain changes to clients. We should set a date for decisions rather than letting rumours run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me build a buffer, but the accounting work itself remains exposed in 2031. Robots in 2034 would change other jobs later, not the tax screens I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would compare approved AI drafts with completed returns each quarter and ask for paid training in tax appeals. If the firm approves the fees and paid hours in writing, I would enroll before 2031. I would build two months of expenses by 2030 if my hours stay whole; in the first year after 2031 I would seek a paid appeals role within the firm if it has a vacancy, while keeping my current clients until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than desperate because I can measure progress each year. I would still check my bank balance before signing up for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quarterly comparison show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count corrected figures, client questions and time saved, then share the page with my team. If the tool gets better, I want to know before the staffing meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you build two months of expenses on your current pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep packing lunches and put bonuses straight into savings, if any bonuses come. The plan fails if my hours slip, so I would review it every quarter.

say: I would propose **dated decisions** about software and staffing to stop rumours.
I would urge the firm to **test drafts** before explaining changes to clients.
think: My **tax desk work** remains exposed when AGI arrives in 2031.
Five years might let me build a **two-month cushion** if hours hold.
do: Compare **approved AI drafts** with completed returns each quarter.
Enroll in **tax appeals training** with employer-funded paid hours; save bonuses toward two months if hours stay whole.
Apply for a vacant **paid appeals** role after 2031 while keeping current clients.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but yearly progress gives me some control.
S3.quote: Robots in 2034 would change other jobs later, not the tax screens I use.
fieldNote: She ties learning to **quarterly evidence** and shares results with the team, which fits her measured approach to new tools.
The **two-month cushion** relies on steady hours and possible bonuses; she names that weakness rather than treating savings as assured.

steps.text: Compare approved AI drafts against completed returns quarterly
Enroll in tax appeals training if firm approves fees and paid hours in writing
Save any bonuses toward two months of expenses if hours stay whole
Apply for vacant paid appeals role after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives the firm a decade to rebuild how we serve clients. I would want younger staff included in those decisions because their first accounting years matter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let me pay down debt and gain experience speaking for clients, but I doubt routine return preparation stays a full career. I may be 37 when the desk work changes, with bills that are larger than today’s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to observe one tax appeal each quarter and test approved tools as they improve, with a senior partner checking the result. I would aim to save four months of expenses by 2035 if my hours stay full; in the first year after 2036, I would take a paid client-advice role only with at least my current salary and written hours, or apply to a vacant nearby compliance team before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point but I have time to build choices. I would not call ten years safe just because it sounds long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan a family differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have no children now, and I would want the savings buffer before taking on a bigger home. I would talk with my partner about timing, not make a promise based on a scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a useful client-advice role pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need at least my current salary and written hours, since the current salary is already low for my job. A new title without paid time would not solve the household problem.

say: I would say **AGI by 2036** gives the firm time to rebuild client service.
I would ask that **younger staff** help decide what the new work looks like.
think: Routine return preparation may not remain a **full career** by 2036.
I could reach age **37** with larger bills and a changed desk job.
do: Observe **one tax appeal** quarterly and test approved tools with partner review.
Save **four months** of expenses by 2035 if my hours stay full, before a larger home.
Take a **client-advice role** after 2036 only with current salary and written hours; otherwise seek a vacant compliance post.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, though the longer runway gives me choices.
S4.quote: A new title without paid time would not solve the household problem.
fieldNote: She links the **decade of preparation** to measured practice, verified AI use and a concrete savings target.
Her **family planning** is cautious: she and her partner have no children and would discuss a larger home only after building savings.

steps.text: Observe one tax appeal each quarter before 2036
Test approved AI tools with senior partner review
Save four months of expenses by 2035 if hours stay full
Take client-advice role only with current salary and written hours; otherwise seek vacant compliance post

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my screen work changes before I can build a rent buffer. A written staffing forecast, paid training, and notice of any hours cut would let me make a real plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who catches the quiet errors after the fast draft is done. The small shop owner cannot audit an automated tax return just because the screen says complete.

headlineQuote: The small shop owner cannot audit an automated tax return just because the screen says complete.
portrait: At **27**, Bianca leads tax and accounts reviews with a master’s degree and chartered accountancy qualification.
Her **senior skill** comes with low pay, less than one month saved, and few similar jobs nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally**, testing approved drafts against real returns before trusting them with client figures.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her; longer runways let her seek paid appeals work and build a conditional savings buffer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her screen-work hours before she can build enough savings for rent.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written staffing forecast**, paid training, and advance notice of any hours cut.
